newsitem.title: USA: The Hartford savors freedom after ITT divorce.
newsitem.headline: The Hartford savors freedom after ITT divorce.

text.p: ITT Hartford's spinoff from ITT Corp. a year ago has allowed the insurer to take charge of its own balance sheet, which has perked up its stock price and reinvigorated the venerable company, seting the stage for sustained growth in 1997, its chairman says.

"The most important scorecard is what's happened to the stock, and the stock is up about 35 percent since we became an independent company," Chairman and Chief Executive Donald Frahm told Reuters in an interview. "That's well in excess of how the market and the insurance industry have moved."

The stock price of ITT Hartford -- the staid company known as "The Hartford," with its famous stag logo -- was above $64 on Friday, compared with below $48 when it ended its 25-year marriage to ITT Corp. last December.

Since the split from ITT, The Hartford has been able to make its own decisions on how to use its capital -- an important issue to insurers, who must constantly tiptoe through volatile claims and industry regulation.
"Being independent has really allowed us to look at the issues of the balance sheet -- capital allocation, capital raising -- with a lot more attention than we had done in the past," said Frahm.

The Hartford -- one of the few diversified insurers left in an era of selloffs and consolidation -- decided to focus in five main areas: life insurance, commercial property-casualty, personal lines property-casualty, reinsurance, and international business.
This year also saw The Hartford exceed $100 billion in assets, placing it among the 25 biggest American companies.

"The (ITT) spinoff energised it, and gave it the opportunity to have stock-type incentives specifically tied to the insurance operation," said Gary Ransom, insurance industry analyst at Conning & Co. in Hartford.
ITT Hartford had revenues of $12.2 billion in 1995, against $11.1 billion in 1994.
Most of its 21,000 employees are in the United States, but the company intends to sniff out growth opportunities in Asia, possibly through acquisition, Frahm said.

"We think our best opportunities as a company are in international (business). We've been expanding primarily in Latin America and Europe ... (but) we're now looking more aggressively at the Far East."
The company aims to push the reinsurance and commercial affinity sides of its business in 1997, said Frahm.
ITT Hartford expects double-digit earnings growth this year and in 1997, he said, without elaborating.
One challenge the company faces is growing its commercial property-casualty business, the most intensely competitive segment of the industry.
The Hartford had $2.8 billion written premiums of commercial property-casualty in 1995, against $2.74 billion in 1994.

"We have not grown in that business," said Frahm. "We now think we've positioned ourselves so that we will be able to out-grow the industry." But he cautioned that the industry growth rate would be "pretty low."
Frahm said that while he did not mean to knock ITT, The Hartford is mulling a name change now that the divorce is a year old.
"It causes confusion," he said of the "ITT Hartford" moniker. "We're addressing that issue right now."
Frahm will end his eight-year reign as chairman on Jan. 31, 1997, a few days after he turns 65.
He will be succeeded by Ramani Ayer, 49, who will become only the ninth chairman in the 186-year-old company's history.
Frahm said he intends to remain on the board of directors "as long as they'll re-elect me."
